newsitem.title: CHINA: World Bank official sees strong China economy.
newsitem.headline: World Bank official sees strong China economy.

text.p: The World Bank's chief of mission in China has said he expects China's strong economic growth to exceed forecasts for this year, but warned of the need to accelerate reform of lumbering state firms and to create more jobs.

"The macro economic situation at this point is very very strong, as inflation has gone down to well below six percent and the economy has been growing at a high but sustainable level," Pieter Bottelier said in an interview with the official Xinhua news agency.

Measures taken in the last three years to rein in the economy have been effective and Beijing's moderately tight fiscal and monetary policies have produced the desired results, resulting in a successful soft landing for the economy last year, he said.
China's economy was expected to improve further this year with major economic indicators very likely to be better than expected, Bottelier said.
China's economy has grown by about 10 percent a year for several years and was expected to show similar growth in 1997 despite an official goal of about 8.0 percent, officials have said.

In addition, Beijing has brought retail price inflation under control, cutting the rate to 6.1 percent last year, down from 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994. China's inflation goal for 1997 is six percent but the figure for the year is expected to be much lower.

However, Bottelier warned of several problems, saying China needed to improve its fiscal situation, accelerate the pace to reform of lumbering state-owned enterprises and the process of commercialising its state-owned banks.

China has been reluctant to leave state firms to sink or swim in a market economy, fearing a stream of bankruptcies and mass unemployment that could spark social unrest. Banking reform has also been hampered by the high level of bad debts extended to the state firms.
Beijing also needed to create more jobs to guarantee healthy and long-term economic development, Bottelier said.
Chinese leaders fear rising unemployment could result in social unrest and protests similar to the student-led demonstrations of 1989 that were suppressed by the army with heavy loss of life.
In terms of the World Bank's role in China, Bottelier said the bank was committed to its projects in China.
"It's... our intention to broaden the range of financial instruments available to support China's development," he was quoted as saying.
Since China resumed World Bank membership in May 1980, it has become the single largest client of the bank with annual borrowings standing at between $2.5 and $3.0 billion.

The bank has lent a total of more than $26.8 billion to 180 projects in China and its lending arm for cheap loans, the International Development Association, plans to arrange more co-financing and cross-financing for China, Bottelier said.
"The World Bank's relationship with China is very effective and we think it is important that the World Bank continues to support social development and poverty elimination in China," he said.
